Indeed, computers are one of God's supremely given blessings to the human being,  to be used or misused according to what is in the hearts of the people.  Now, God ordained that the computer would be the final scripture he would give us.  And because his plan was that 14 centuries later,  he was going to allow the people to discover how to make and use computers. All of these are only possible for us to do because of the computer.  The computer also allows us to wage nuclear war.  Now, we know all this new knowledge would overwhelm the people.  God knew that all this new knowledge would overwhelm the people  and even make people suppose that they had discovered the computer independently of God's will  and even forget God entirely.  God wanted to reassure the believers who would be living in such a fantastically new world  as opened by the computer and as we're seeing unveiled to us all around every day.  God wanted to let us know, us people who are living in the age of computers,  to clearly know that he fully controls the computers along with the rest of his creation.  Alhamdulillah. This is exactly what surah 57 told us about the purpose of iron and technology.  And God put a coded message in the Koran, his final scripture,  that could be found and appreciated only after the computer was invented.  In this way, God not only proves to us that he has preserved the written integrity of the Koran,  every word, every letter.  As has been discussed here many times,  he proves to us that he controls the computer, which was needed to make this discovery.  Now we should appreciate the exact timing by which the computer message was delivered.  Now if we look back at just the recent history of the computer itself,  in the 1940s and 1950s, the modern computer was just being developed.  And it was going from having some mechanical gears to all electronics.  First using the big old vacuum tubes and finally transistors.  Now these were called first and second generation computers  and only a few hundred or a few thousand could be made.  They were very expensive and they needed a room the size of a gymnasium to house them.  Then in the mid-1950s and early 60s, miniature circuits and microchips began to be developed.  These became the third generation computers.  Now these are the large ones that are used by universities and businesses.  And they process information thousands of times faster than the original computers.  This is the kind of computer that Ustadz Kalitza was using  when he first discovered the miracle in the Quran.  This is the kind of computer they have over here at the University Computer Center.  But the little computers, the ones you see back in the office,  the ones you see advertised on TV and in the magazines,  the computer scientists call these fourth generation computers.  And they represent the real computer revolution.  They've only been commercially available the last three or four years  and only in the last year or so at prices that very many people could afford.  Some now are only a hundred to three or four hundred dollars  and you just hook them up to a TV set.  Now we can notice that this timing coincides with the publication of Ustadz's translation of the Quran  and the proliferation of the information about the 19 codes in the Quran itself.  His book, The Computer Speaks, and his other books.  Now the mathematical miracle of the Quran, of course,  isn't only to be studied and appreciated by people who have access to big computers  in universities or IBM or such places.  It's to be appreciated by everyone.  And though we don't need a computer to appreciate the miracle of the Quran itself,  with or without knowledge of the codes,  the fact is that the computer is affecting so many people's lives.  And so the appreciation of the code through the computer is very important, I think.  Since God exactly timed the release of the computer miracle in the Quran,  he also planned the exact timing of the release of these many computers  and the availability to everyone. But as I've been typing it,  I do read the Arabic text.  And I get used to words and patterns  and I compare it with the English text  which is there in my Quran beside it.  So I am learning more vocabulary as I go along.  Even with only partly understanding the Arabic,  sometimes I really get choked up  just in the sense of it's totally different than reading the translation.  Sometimes I'll be typing along  and just typing in letters  and just reading words without thinking about it.  And it's something that will kind of jump at me.  And I'll start wondering what's being said here  and then I'll go and look at the English text.  And it's kind of a strange experience.  Even without understanding the actual meanings of many of the words,  I became to recognize many of them  just because they are repeated over and over. It seemed to me not only are there rhythms  when we hear the Quran in sight,  but there are patterns in the letters themselves.  And because of this experience,  I am more convinced not only that the choices of words  and spelling in the Quran are designed to accommodate the 19 code,  but every word and every letter is chosen and placed  exactly for a specific purpose.  Now, when I read the Quran,  I'm reminded of patterns and rules of logic  which I learned in computer programming.  Well, I can't offer you any specific evidence for this statement.  I will only offer you some of the thoughts that I've had.  That leads me to make this kind of statement.  We're all aware that the Quran is written in an unusual style,  unlike any other book.  It's almost the first thing that everyone notices  when they're reading the Quran for the first time.  We find a few verses talking about one subject,  and then suddenly the next verse seems to be talking about  some entirely different subject.  We find ourselves jumping to verses in other sources  scattered all over the Quran to continue learning  additional information on a specific subject.  This is not the style of an ordinary book  of literature, philosophy, or poetry,  where the writer keeps the subject's development  following a linear sequence of logic.  It is very much the style of a complex computer program.  Which sends the computer jumping around  to different sets of instructions  and other parts of the program from back and forth.  In order for the computer to keep track  of where it should go for the next step,  the program uses numbers and specific names as addresses  so the computer will not get lost.  Now, when we're reading the Quran,  we sometimes find the same verse numbers  in different suras are talking about the same subject.  And it reminds me of this aspect of the computer program. For example, the electric company  might use a computer card  with a bunch of holes in it  to process our electric bill.  Now, one set of holes in that computer card  tells the computer the customer number.  Now, every customer has a different number.  So the program has to tell the computer  that we're still talking about the same thing.  And it calls that set of holes  wherever the number is  as a customer number. And even though there are other possible words  in the Arabic that could be used,  the Quran always sticks with the word ayat  for uses consistent.  Whether the ayat we're talking about  is the parting of the sea from Moses,  or the creation,  the pattern of the sun and the moon  around each other,  the signs that Moses showed to Pharaoh,  the letters in the suras are called ayat,  the verses that were sent down were called ayat,  the sending of the rain to go to the crops  was called ayat.  Now, there's many, many examples.  Now, they're all named ayat  so that we can understand that all these different signs  and miracles are for one purpose.  They're proof of God's power over everything.  Surah 6, verse 105,  Thus do we bury the signs, the ayat,  to let them realize you have learned,  and we explain the signs to the people who have knowledge.  Well, I hope I haven't been too long and confusing in this.  Certainly my own experience of working on the computer  makes me appreciate even more the miracles  that have been told in the Quran  and how complex and difficult Dr. Kaliqa's own work was.  And really, you couldn't have discovered it by intention, I don't think.  And it makes me appreciate even more  just how extraordinary and inexhaustible the Quran itself is.  It becomes really attempting to go far afield  in exploring the technical structure of the Quran,  how many letters and words there are,  and the choice of words, the arrangement of verses,  and suras, and much, much more.  But really, the important thing in the end  is what was important in the first place,  is to believe and worship God.  And we should strive to understand  what the words of the Quran say,  telling us how to worship God  and how the believer should treat one another.  All this elaboration and mathematical detail  may occupy our minds like a great puzzle,  but if this is the nature of our minds,  it's the way God designed them.  Still, in the end, what we are learning  is nothing more than we bore witness to  at a creation.  There is no God but God,  so let us worship God alone and work righteousness.  Bismillahir Rahmanir Rahim  Alhamdulillah  Bismillahir Rahmanir Rahim  Bismillahir Rahmanir Rahim Last updated 11 months ago
